name: Bridge
intent: Split a class into two independent hierarchies, an abstraction and an implementation, so each can vary on its own.
scenario: Remote controls (basic, advanced) operate devices (TV, radio). Any remote should work with any device.
problem: You have two ways of varying: the kind of remote and the kind of device. Subclassing every pair (TvBasicRemote, TvAdvancedRemote, RadioBasicRemote...) multiplies classes. Adding one device means adding a class for every remote type.
solution: Keep the remote hierarchy and the device hierarchy separate. A remote holds a reference to a Device interface and delegates the real work to it. That reference is the bridge. New remotes and new devices are added independently.
pain: One class per remote and device pair: 2 x 2 = 4 classes already
A new device means a new class for every remote type
A new remote type means a new class for every device
Remote logic is copied across the pair classes
benefits: Remotes and devices are separate hierarchies
2 remotes + 3 devices = 5 classes, not 6, and the gap grows
A new device works with every existing remote
Swap the device behind a remote at runtime
whenToUse: A class varies along two independent dimensions
You want to switch implementations at runtime
Both abstraction and implementation should be extensible by subclassing
whenNotToUse: Only one dimension varies: plain inheritance or Strategy is enough
The abstraction and implementation are tightly coupled by nature
The extra indirection is not worth it for a small, stable class set
pitfalls: Hard to see the need up front: it is usually a refactor from a class explosion
The implementor interface must be designed with care: too fat and every device must fake features
Easy to confuse with Adapter (which retrofits) and Strategy (which swaps one behaviour)
More objects to wire together at start-up

roles.label: Abstraction
roles.description: High-level control that holds a reference to the implementor.

roles.label: Refined Abstraction
roles.description: Extends the abstraction with more features.

roles.label: Concrete Implementor
roles.description: A real device implementing those operations.

quiz.question: A drawing app has 3 shapes (circle, square, triangle) and 4 renderers (SVG, canvas, PDF, OpenGL), built as one subclass per shape and renderer pair. A fifth renderer is requested. How many new classes does that take, with the pair-subclass design versus a Bridge?
options: 1 new class with pairs, 1 with a Bridge
3 new classes with pairs, 3 with a Bridge
3 new classes with pairs, 1 with a Bridge
5 new classes with pairs, 3 with a Bridge
quiz.explanation: With a pair per combination, each of the 3 shapes needs a class for the new renderer, so 3. With a Bridge, shapes hold a Renderer interface, so only one new renderer class is needed and every shape works with it.

quiz.question: An Invoice class must be exported as PDF, CSV or JSON, and the user picks the format on each request. There is only one kind of document and none is planned. Which design fits best?
options: An Adapter around each export library, with Invoice picking one by class name at request time
A full Bridge, with an Invoice hierarchy and a Document hierarchy, so a second document type is cheap later
One Invoice class whose export method switches on a format string and holds all three writers
Invoice takes an Exporter interface with three implementations, and the format is passed in per request
quiz.explanation: Only one dimension varies, so a plain interface that is injected is enough, and it also allows a runtime choice. A Bridge pays for a second hierarchy that nothing needs, and the switch makes Invoice grow with every new format.

quiz.question: In a Bridge, the Device implementor interface has powerOn, setVolume, setChannel, setStation and setBrightness. The Radio throws 'not supported' from setChannel and setBrightness, and every new device does the same. What is the best fix?
options: Document which methods each device throws on, and have the remotes catch those errors
Add a RadioRemote subclass for each device type, so the remote knows what each device supports
Make Radio's unsupported methods do nothing, so remotes can call them without risk
Shrink the interface to primitives every device has, and let remotes build richer actions
quiz.explanation: A fat implementor forces devices to fake features. A small set of primitives keeps the bridge honest, and remotes compose them into richer behaviour. Catching or ignoring the calls hides the problem, and per-device remotes bring back the class explosion.
